The post WEEKEND READING: HERA 2.0: aligning higher education regulation with England’s integrated skills economy appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Dave Phoenix, Vice-Chancellor of The Open University.

The Higher Education and Research Act (HERA) 2017 fundamentally reshaped the English higher education system. It introduced a regulatory framework centred on competition, student choice and market entry, underpinned by the belief that a well-regulated market would drive innovation, improve quality and deliver better outcomes for students. The Office for Students (OfS) was established to oversee this approach through a risk-based model of regulation.

Nearly a decade later, however, both the sector and the wider policy environment have changed significantly. This raises an important question: Can a regulatory framework designed primarily to promote competition between providers provide the right incentives at a time when government increasingly expects the sector to operate as part of an integrated tertiary education and skills system?

The limitations of a market-based regulatory model

The current system rightly uses measurable outcomes, including continuation, completion, graduate outcomes and financial sustainability, to inform regulation. But metrics shape behaviour. Where continuation and retention become central measures of success, providers will naturally focus on protecting those indicators.

Meanwhile, the provider landscape has become more complex. Diversity can bring innovation, but a more heterogeneous sector requires more sophisticated quality assurance, particularly where different provider cultures may respond differently to regulatory incentives, undermining the use of outcome measures as sole measures of risk.

Furthermore, the Post-16 Education and Skills White Paper, Local Skills Improvement Plans, devolution reforms and the Lifelong Learning Entitlement all point towards a future in which learners move more flexibly between technical, professional and academic routes. Success is increasingly defined by the effectiveness of the system as a whole, not simply by the performance of individual institutions in isolation.

These changes create two challenges for the current framework:

First, recognition that educational quality cannot be captured through metrics alone. Quality includes academic standards, intellectual challenge, curriculum design, assessment integrity, access to resources, student support and the wider environment in which learners develop knowledge, skills and confidence. If institutions focus on meeting a measure rather than sustaining the underlying academic environment, the ability of current metrics to assess sector risk is reduced.

Second, while the framework largely evaluates individual institutions, the skills agenda requires universities, colleges and employers to build coherent pathways and respond collectively to regional and national needs, which isn’t currently a focus of the framework.

These tensions are visible in debates about minimum entry requirements for access to funding, which seek to address institutional behaviour through additional headline thresholds rather than concerns around the underlying conditions of quality. At the same time, less attention has been given to the system-wide impact of losing key subject provision as financial pressures drive course closures, creating cold spots and impacting equity of opportunity.

The case for HERA 2.0

HERA 2.0 should preserve robust accountability while broadening regulation from institutional compliance towards educational quality, public value, collaboration and system stewardship. In this context, HERA 2.0 would need to reflect three shifts.

1. Quality review

Risk-based regulation should continue to use data on continuation, completion, graduate outcomes and financial resilience. A stronger model would combine absolute thresholds with two additional elements:

Use of benchmark data including contextual and value-added measures reflecting students’ starting points, mode of study, subject mix, socio-economic background, prior attainment and engagement. This would show whether providers are generating strong outcomes relative to the learners they serve, rather than judging all institutions against crude sector averages. In effect this would create a value-added metric that asks not only whether students complete, but how completion is achieved and what educational gain has occurred, as already occurs in other parts of the educational sector. Benchmarks would support a risk-based methodology in which significant variations could trigger quality review by subject experts, as currently.

Use of peer review as seen in Scotland’s Tertiary Quality Enhancement Review. International practice also points in this same direction. Australia’s TEQSA model is standards-based and risk-reflective, combining data with scrutiny of governance, staffing, facilities, student support and academic integrity. These systems do not abandon metrics; they embed them in a wider evidence base about the educational processes behind the numbers.

Independent peer review would provide judgements on quality and standards, while thematic reviews could examine issues raised by absolute or value-added metrics, including franchised provision, subject withdrawal, online delivery, assessment integrity, unusual completion patterns and work-based learning. This would therefore build on current work and could cover:

quality, integrity, breadth and depth of academic provision;

learner progression and successful outcomes;

educational gain; and

financial sustainability and governance.

2. Ensuring public benefit in exchange for public investment

Where institutions draw on public funding, taxpayer-backed student finance or public regulatory legitimacy, the test should extend beyond acceptable educational outcomes for individual students. Public investment in higher education should also secure wider public benefit: national capability, regional growth, expanded opportunity, international influence, strategically important provision and contribution to civic, cultural and economic life, for example.

The broader provider landscape created by HERA has brought diversity and innovation, but it has also exposed the limits of relying on market entry and a narrow set of performance metrics as proxies for public purpose. A system that attaches public funding mainly to recruitment and minimum outcomes risks rewarding providers whose incentive is to capture publicly backed income rather than contribute to long-term public value.

HERA 2.0 should therefore introduce a public value framework for all providers. Assessment should consider whether public funding supports activity that a purely commercial market would underprovide. This could take into account the provider’s mission and consider a basket of measures including, for example:

employer engagement, labour market relevance and contribution to skills priorities;

support for underserved communities and cold spots

contribution to inward investment, innovation ecosystems, international partnerships and soft power; and

civic engagement and wider national capability in terms of subject coverage and underpinning research.

This would set a clearer test for access to public funding, as providers would have to show that they deliver public benefit beyond private return. That would make the system less attractive to organisations focused only on extracting profit from publicly backed student finance, while supporting any provider that can evidence quality, integrity, sustainability and contribution to national or local priorities.

3. Supporting an integrated skills system

If government wants a coherent tertiary education system, the legislative framework should actively support collaboration rather than treat it as incidental. A more integrated system depends on a diversity of mission, with different providers contributing distinctive strengths to progression, local skills, research and innovation, professional education, work-based learning and lifelong learning.

Institutions could be encouraged to develop progression agreements with colleges, support credit transfer and recognition of prior learning, create flexible routes into higher-level study and recognise work with employers to keep provision aligned with labour market needs in line with their mission. The framework could therefore consider approaches to:

Credit recognition

Pathway development through flexible or local routes into and through higher education

Research and innovation capability.

Conclusion

HERA responded to the priorities of its time. But policy environments change,and regulatory frameworks must evolve with them. England’s challenge is no longer simply how to regulate a higher education market, but how to build a tertiary education and skills system that supports growth, productivity, social mobility and lifelong learning. This is only going to become more complex as evolution seeks to balance national and local oversight around education, research and innovation needs

HERA 2.0 would retain institutional accountability while restoring an element of professional judgement, strengthening protection for students and public investment, and moving quality assurance beyond compliance towards educational enhancement. It would link access to public funding not just to regulatory compliance, but to demonstrable quality, learner success and public value.

It would also align regulation with a government agenda founded on skills, growth, opportunity and collaboration: moving beyond oversight of a market of competing institutions towards stewardship of an integrated system in which universities, colleges, employers and regional partners work together to expand opportunity and strengthen productivity. If the ambitions of the next decade are growth, skills, opportunity and lifelong learning, the regulatory framework should evolve to support them.

title: ‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disowned | Alexander Hurst
summary:
Fixing the broken education system will be just the start. The biggest challenge for an aloof political class is to finally pay attention to an abandoned generation

When adolescents protest that the government is failing to uphold their right to an education, and the government’s response is to send in riot police, the government has lost the plot. People outside France may have spent the past week watching the student protests in Paris and other cities, and thought, “Well, France has a long tradition of insurrection” or, “That’s just the French being French.”

But the situation that has provoked the high-school walkouts and teenage anger is most likely not one they would immediately associate with the France of their imaginations. In place of its lost plot, the French government has a collection of anecdotes and statistics that it should be ashamed of: 27th place in the most recent OECD education rankings, schools with ceilings collapsing and rats in classrooms and, in a school in Bagnolet, no drinkable water; an increase in the average number of students per class from 27 in 2010 to over 30 today; half of primary and high schools missing teachers at the start of the school year – many of them with no substitutes or replacements.

Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoir Generation Desperation is out now

full_text:
When adolescents protest that the government is failing to uphold their right to an education, and the government’s response is to send in riot police, the government has lost the plot. People outside France may have spent the past week watching the student protests in Paris and other cities, and thought, “Well, France has a long tradition of insurrection” or, “That’s just the French being French.”

But the situation that has provoked the high-school walkouts and teenage anger is most likely not one they would immediately associate with the France of their imaginations. In place of its lost plot, the French government has a collection of anecdotes and statistics that it should be ashamed of: 27th place in the most recent OECD education rankings, schools with ceilings collapsing and rats in classrooms and, in a school in Bagnolet, no drinkable water; an increase in the average number of students per class from 27 in 2010 to over 30 today; half of primary and high schools missing teachers at the start of the school year – many of them with no substitutes or replacements.

Julie, a 34-year-old teacher who joined the demonstrations, told me that staff shortages were the fault of “low salaries and poor treatment.” She has to commute for an hour and 45 minutes each way between Paris and the school on the city’s outskirts where she accepted a post last year after switching careers. All for €2100 (£1,780) a month, plus some overtime pay. Teachers’ salaries in France are only 56% of what they are in Germany – even as over €200bn in public subsidies finds its way annually to businesses.

So it could easily have been a teacher-led revolt – instead, the high-schoolers themselves cracked first.

They paid a high price for refusing to accept a failing education system: a 16-year-old has lost the use of an eye, a 15-year-old has lost a hand, a 14-year-old has a broken jaw – all from police munitions. Hundreds more have been injured in some way. In total, 4,400 people, the vast majority minors, have been arrested in a little over a week, almost half the number of arrests made during the months of gilets jaunes chaos. It might be incoherent that protesting students shoot fireworks at high school buildings, while at the same time denouncing the poor facilities they have to study in. But the far greater incoherence belongs to a government that has disinvested in its youth, and has chosen to answer bin fires with police charges.

“Sure some people were burning trash cans,” Fatoumata Sylla Wague, a 17-year-old in her final year at the Lycée Paul Éluard in Seine-Saint-Denis, where pupils were among the first to set up blockades outside their campus, told me. “But trash cans can’t feel anything.” She and her fellow students, on the other hand, certainly felt the teargas that the police launched in response.

Despite “unlivable” temperatures in the school buildings, extreme heat and extreme cold, walls covered in mould, electricity cuts and often not enough tables or chairs for everyone, Fatoumata would rather have been in class than out braving the riot police. But she wants to teach history some day and felt compelled, in a moment in history, comparable to May 1968, to take part. “If I’m fighting for our rights today, it’s because I really want to teach, but in good conditions. And so this is for the next generation of students and teachers.”

I can’t imagine how hard it must be to be a teenager in general today. In 2021 The Lancet found that 75% of French 16-25-year-olds exhibited signs of eco-anxiety, telling researchers they were “frightened” about the future. In France and beyond, students and young workers actively dislike AI and feel pessimistic about the future it portends. As for Fatoumata, she worries about the rise of far-right political movements, both in France and elsewhere.

For years, successive French governments have dealt with problems in some of France’s most troubled urban areas by unleashing heavy-handed policing that all too frequently targets young people with random checks that can be personally degrading. Centralised policymaking has also produced a national education system that often sends its least experienced teachers to these same areas, while granting more senior teachers priority in requesting transfers to other, less difficult, schools.

A future far-right government, the kind Fatoumata says she worries about, would almost certainly ramp up these kinds of tensions. Already, in response to the protests, rightwing politicians have called for harsher sentences and more law and order. But this is not a problem that will be solved with more police and more batons, any more than it already has been.

Because none of it signals a government that truly wants to listen – it signals that society at large does not really claim these places, or these teenagers, as its own. On n’est pas mal éduqué, on n’est pas écouté (“We’re not poorly educated, we’re just not being listened to”), read one sign I saw brandished at Paris’s Place de la République on Tuesday.

Responding to the crisis is going to require some tangible acts, such as upgrading dilapidated facilities. Arnaud Richards, 50, head of student services at Iqbal Masih middle school in Saint-Denis, offered me the example of how thoughtful architecture can have more impact than one might expect. The technical high school he previously worked in – Gabriel Péri, in an extremely poor area – reopened in 2022 after a total reconstruction, which, according to Richards, led to a calmer climate for both students and teachers. “Having the school itself be a beautiful place made the community feel more respected,” he told me. That in turn “created a calmer environment” for both students and staff.

But a real answer doesn’t stop with better facilities. Showing up to cut ribbons on new construction, or renovations, isn’t enough. During Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power, his government has, on any number of issues, successively failed to listen in a way that makes people feel deeply seen and heard.

As Fatoumata said: “Honestly, I don’t think the government cares, they just want to shut us up with false promises. We know nothing will change, because the government doesn’t listen to us.” Of all the things going wrong for France at the moment, this underlying lack of a feeling of “togetherness”, the feeling that nobody is really listening, is going to be the most difficult to deal with.

title: The Uneven Payoff of Returning to College
summary:
The Uneven Payoff of Returning to College
Joshua.Bay Fri, 10/09/2026 - 03:00 AM

A new report from California Competes finds that adults who return to college and graduate report benefits beyond earnings, but debt and local job opportunities impact their returns.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Roughly 43 million Americans have some college credits but no credential, including about 37 million working-age adults under 65. Re-engaging these adults could expand economic opportunities and help address workforce shortages, but new research suggests the financial benefits of completing a degree vary considerably among those who return to college.

A new report from California Competes, part of its ongoing Degrees of Value research series, examines the return on investment of a college degree among adults who previously stopped out and later graduated. Drawing on interviews with 27 California adult learners who left college and later returned, researchers explored the financial, personal and social benefits of completing a degree, as well as the costs associated with returning to college. Participants were first interviewed in 2023 and again in 2025.

About half of the graduates interviewed saw their earnings increase within three years of completing their degrees, particularly those who returned with clear career goals. One graduate went from earning $10 an hour as a cleaner at a nursing facility to more than $100,000 annually as a nurse. But graduates in rural communities described more limited financial gains because of fewer local job opportunities.

Emi Fujita-Conrads, a researcher at California Competes and author of the report, said graduates with clear career goals were often encouraged by their employers to return to college. Those facing limited job opportunities in their communities, however, could benefit from earlier career advising and better information about regional labor markets, she said.

“Adult learners really need clear and early career guidance,” Fujita-Conrads said. “Students are getting career guidance, but it often arrives too late to make informed choices.”

Benefits and barriers: While traditional measures of college return on investment focus on the economic benefits of earning a degree relative to its costs, the report takes a broader approach, examining the financial, personal and social benefits of completing college, as well as the financial, opportunity and personal costs.

The report found that the value of completing a degree extended beyond higher earnings. Graduates described developing stronger skills, gaining greater self-confidence, broadening their perspectives and creating better opportunities for their children.

“We find that institutions tend to focus resources on what’s measured, and it’s important to track earnings and economic outcomes,” Fujita-Conrads said. “But if California continues to only track earnings, we’ll miss these outcomes that students really value.”

Returning to college also came with significant costs. Some graduates reported accumulating $80,000 to $100,000 in debt. Others described forgone wages, childcare expenses and the challenges of balancing work, family and school.

“We saw that some of these added costs were around losing credits and extending the time to a degree, which pushed students into additional debt,” Fujita-Conrads said. “This was even more important for adults, too … where adults could be working but were instead attending school, studying and commuting to classes.”

Other research suggests that adults who leave college without a credential continue to see value in earning a degree, even when financial and personal challenges stand in their way. A report from Trellis Strategies, based on a survey of more than 3,000 former undergraduates across 58 institutions in 13 states, found that 73 percent believed completing their degree would improve their career earnings and potential, while 70 percent believed it would provide a higher quality of life.

Yet those expectations coexist with significant barriers to completion. Among respondents who identified reasons for leaving college, 35 percent cited personal finances, 32 percent said family or personal responsibilities, 27 percent cited employment and 25 percent attributed it to the cost of attendance.

Maximizing degree value: The report recommends steps state policymakers and higher education leaders can take to strengthen the benefits of a degree and reduce the barriers adults face, including providing better local labor market data, expanding credit for prior learning and removing age restrictions on Cal Grants.

Fujita-Conrads said providing adult learners with earlier career guidance and information about regional employment opportunities could help them make more informed decisions about their education and whether their credentials will lead to the outcomes they hope to achieve.

“Students who entered with a clear sense of how their credential was going to lead to their goals and their career outcomes—and whether those opportunities existed within their region—were able to see those benefits from a college degree,” Fujita-Conrads said.

“Listening to students is a really key part in understanding what the return on investment of college is, and what students really want when they go back to school,” she added.

title: University of Colorado Denver to Open Branch Campus in India
summary:
University of Colorado Denver to Open Branch Campus in India
Susan H. Greenberg Fri, 10/09/2026 - 03:00 AM

The research institution will be the first public American university to offer U.S. degrees on Indian soil.

Byline(s)
Rosalind Skillen for Times Higher Education
full_text:
The University of Colorado Denver has become the first public American university authorized to establish a campus in India, with the first cohort of students expected to begin their studies in August 2027.

CU Denver has received a letter of intent from India’s University Grants Commission (UGC) to open a base in Hyderabad. If the deal is approved by the institution's accreditor, the Higher Learning Commission, CU Denver would be the first foreign university to launch in the state of Telangana in south-central India.

The university would also be the first public American institution to launch on Indian soil. A private institution, the Illinois Institute of Technology, welcomed its inaugural cohort of students to its campus in Vikhroli, Mumbai, this year.

Telangana is one of India’s fastest-growing technology hubs, with a booming pharmaceutical sector and thriving start-up culture.

According to CU Denver, the Hyderabad location will “offer pathways for students in high-demand fields including business, computing, engineering and analytics.” The university has said that additional programs will be proposed to India’s UGC for approval in year two and beyond.

“Expanding access to high-quality education has long been central to CU Denver’s vision and goals,” Chancellor Kenneth T. Christensen said in a press statement. “Our plans in Hyderabad build on that commitment, as well as our longstanding connection with students from India who have been part of the CU Denver community for decades.”

The chancellor said establishing a presence in India represents an “opportunity to extend that connection” and “bring our unique experience to students in India.”

Rahul Choudaha, the director of DrEducation Research, said Hyderabad is “a strategic and competitive choice” on the part of CU Denver, “as it offers a relatively lower cost base as compared to Mumbai or Bengaluru, and hence can offer programs at a lower tuition price point.”

Choudaha has previously argued that getting the pricing of a branch campus right is “critical” to the long-term success of overseas ventures.

He added that, as the first university in Hyderabad, CU Denver may also be able to capture a “bigger local and regional student base” compared with the five campuses in competition with one another in Mumbai.

CU Denver has chosen the global education company Emeritus as a joint venture partner in the overseas initiative.

Ashwin Damera, CEO of Emeritus, said that the new campus “marks an important step in bringing globally relevant education closer to students in India.”

“CU Denver’s focus on applied learning, interdisciplinary education, and career readiness is particularly relevant to the aspirations of today’s students and the needs of a rapidly evolving workforce,” said Damera.

“The initiative will create opportunities for students and provide greater access to an education that is both academically rigorous and closely connected to the world of work.”

Editor's note: This article has been updated to clarify that the campus's accreditation authorization and approval from the Higher Learning Commission is pending.

title: Whac-a-Mole Revisited
summary:
Whac-a-Mole Revisited
Sara Brady Fri, 10/09/2026 - 03:00 AM

The more things change …

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
It was quite a month this week. After the third or fourth reference I heard to Whac-a-mole, it occurred to me that I had written on it before, when I worked at another college. The piece is below. The particulars have changed—it was written right before the start of the semester, for one thing—but the big picture holds up. Some things don’t change.

Whack-a-mole is a game wherein you have a mallet, and you stand facing some “ground” with a bunch of holes in it. Each hole contains a mechanical mole, and they pop up at random intervals. Your job is to hit each mole on the head as quickly as possible when it pops up. It’s remarkably satisfying.

The real life version is satisfying, too, when it works. At least for a little while.

Befitting the last moments before classes start and the onslaught hits, emergencies popped up all day. An adjunct backed out! The server is down! Two key people are suddenly fighting!

Typically, half the battle is getting everyone to calm down long enough to get the full picture.

When things get abruptly weird, there’s usually a temptation to just solve it. Just do it. And in rare cases—small child obliviously in path of oncoming car, say—that’s the right response. Whack the mole and don’t waste time thinking.

But here, most of the time, abrupt solutions cause more issues than they solve. The adjunct backed out? Just give the class to so-and-so! But then so-and-so doesn’t want it, and someone else did, and why weren’t they considered, and this has happened before, and The Administration has its favorites, and …

No, no, no.

I don’t know the psychological principle behind it, but when stressed, most people seem to develop a sort of tunnel vision. That one mole looms large, and they can’t see anything else.

But focusing on one mole is a guaranteed way to lose the game. There are always more moles out there. The trick is not to lose sight of them. In this setting, that means stepping back for a moment, bouncing ideas off other people and coming up with something beyond the unthinking response.

It’s even worse with interpersonal conflict. Some of the behind-the-scenes people are running pretty ragged right now and having a hard time keeping up with everything that has to get squared away before classes start. Unfortunately, one person’s third priority is another one’s first, and the latter is getting pretty annoyed at the former. Under stress, even good people quickly resort to escalating blame, since in their frustration they don’t consider other explanations. (To be fair, I do this with other drivers all the time.) Blaming causes CYA behavior, which leads to avoidance, which means the problem gets worse, which leads to more blaming … Again, no, no, no.

In these situations, you have to do a tricky two-step: acknowledge the frustration and urgency, then get everyone to take a step back anyway. That’s what my day of whack-a-mole has been. It’s closer to “hostage negotiator” than “firefighter.” Yesterday, it worked. Today, we’ll see …

Sixteen years later, and 16 years older, it’s pretty much right. The more fraught the situation, the more important not to get consumed by it. If you lose the plot, the moles can whack you.

title: After days of giving French-only answers in legislature, Kinew wants schools to cover '80s language battle
summary: Manitoba's premier wants the province's schools to teach students about the intense public backlash to the expansion of francophone rights in the 1980s.
full_text:
Manitoba's premier wants the schools in the province to teach students about the bitter fight against the expansion of francophone rights in the 1980s.

Premier Wab Kinew is calling for the addition to the education curriculum, after his decision to speak almost exclusively in French during four days of question period at the legislature was celebrated by some and questioned by others.

He also said he'd like to see a live translation of question period offered for people watching online — which the legislative assembly is working on.

"I hope that after this week, we can use this experience as motivation to renew our education system to share our own history as Manitoba, including those struggles and challenges for the Francophonie to protect your language and your culture," Kinew told host Jérémy Laniel in a Friday French-language interview with Le 6 à 9, Radio-Canada's morning radio show in Manitoba.

Kinew was referring to the French-language crisis of the 1980s, when a government bill calling for provincial services to be offered in French sparked an outcry and protests from some English-speakers.

Th e offices of the Société de la francophonie manitobaine were targeted by an arson , and the opposition Progressive Conservatives spent nearly two weeks blocking a vote on the government bill.

The NDP government succumbed to the public pressure, withdrawing the bill in 1984.

By the next year, however, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled Manitoba's unilingual laws were unconstitutional. The laws needed to be translated into French to be re-enacted, the court ruled.

Kinew said many Manitobans aren't aware of this history.

"The reality in Manitoba is that the French language is the language of your mothers, your fathers, your grandparents. And then they had to hide their books, they had to hide their signs with French text," he said in French.

Kinew said the government would consult with the Franco-Manitoban School Division, Société de la francophonie manitobaine and other experts who understand that history before incorporating it into the curriculum.

Bernard Lesage, board chair of the French-language school division, said he's pleased that if the changes are approved, all students will get to learn more about Franco-Manitoban history.

Criticized for French answers

Since La Vérendrye MLA Konrad Narth was appointed interim leader of the Opposition Progressive Conservatives two weeks ago, Kinew has answered every English-language question put to him in the legislature in French.

In late May, Narth — who doesn't speak French — got into hot water when he was overheard saying Kinew showed a "basic lack of respect" for responding to his question in French.

Narth later said he asked the question in English, not French, prompting heckling from NDP MLAs who accused him of disrespecting the language, according to an audio recording of the exchange.

He later apologized for how his comments came across. Narth also said he appreciates that he can ask questions in the language he's most comfortable in, and Kinew can respond in French with translation available to all MLAs.

The premier has denied that he's speaking French in the chamber because of Narth's actions from May. He told reporters this week Narth was "disrespecting the bilingual tradition."

By Friday, Kinew suggested he feels "a bit like Forrest Gump" — the movie character famed for going on an epic cross-country run "for no particular reason."

Kinew said he started speaking French, "and then I thought it was important to keep going. But I don't really know the exact reason."

Kinew has previously spoken French in the legislature but usually only regarding francophone matters.

Boosting national profile: political scientist

He disagreed Friday that he is politicizing the use of French, as Raymond Hébert, a professor emeritus of political studies who wrote a book on Manitoba's French-language crisis, has suggested.

Hébert also said the premier's conduct might undermine his government's efforts to advance bilingualism by antagonizing anglophones.

Kinew said he respects Hébert, but "Manitoba has changed a lot," pointing to growth in French-immersion scho ols and the many people who speak and respect the language and its history.

His NDP gove rnment has vowed to make the province a "truly bilingual" province. The province consulted with people last year, and a provincial strategy is scheduled for release in March 2027.

While Manitoba's courts and legislature operate in English and French, other government services are offered in both languages only in designated areas where there is a "concentrated" francophone population. The province is not officially bilingual by law.

A political scientist in Quebec suggested Kinew's use of French in the legislature may be about more than scoring political points or appealing to Franco-Manitobans.

"I think that is someone who might have national ambitions, and certainly someone who has a national profile" as a popular premier, said Daniel Béland, director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada.

"Showing to the rest of the country, and including to people in Quebec, that he speaks French … increases his profile across the country."

Kinew also told Radio-Canada he doesn't think it "would be a huge deal" to offer live translation of question period. MLAs already receive a translation through an earpiece on their desks.

He said those decisions are up to the legislature's Speaker, who, earlier this year, made picture-in-picture American Sign Language interpretation available during all question period broadcasts.

Rick Yarish, clerk of the legislative assembly, said the legislature doesn't currently have the technological capacities to provide the translation but is working to implement the service. No timeline is available.

He said the goal is to have a second video feed of question period airing exclusively on the assembly's broadcast page, which would include a live translation of French spoken in the chamber to English. The primary video feed, featuring whichever language is being spoken, would remain as is and broadcast simultaneously on YouTube.

title: Residential school denialism shouldn't be illegal, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says
summary: Residential school denialism is detestable but not illegal, and that shouldn't change, says Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who disagrees with federal Manitoba NDPer Leah Gazan's efforts to add it to the Criminal Code.
full_text:
Residential school denialism is detestable but not illegal, and that shouldn't change, says Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who disagrees with federal Manitoba NDPer Leah Gazan's efforts to add it to the Criminal Code.

"I have a lot of respect for MP Gazan, but I don't think we can criminalize this. I think we have to just do the continued work of educating people and trying to combat misinformation," Kinew told CBC Manitoba Up to Speed host Marcy Markusa on Friday.

Gazan first introduced Bill C-254, her private member’s bill to amend the Criminal Code regarding the promotion of hatred against Indigenous people, in October 2024, but it died when the spring 2025 election was called.

"If the government is serious about reconciliation, then they need to protect survivors and their families from hate," Gazan said when she first introduced it.

"The residential school system was a genocide designed to wipe out Indigenous cultures, languages, families and heritage. To downplay, deny or justify it is cruel, harmful and hateful."

She reintroduced it in October 2025. The bill seeks to make it illegal for anyone to condone, deny, justify or minimize the Indian residential school system in Canada through any statements beyond a private conversation.

All bills must go through three readings, which also involves committee reviews and final debates, before being granted royal assent and enacted into law.

The introduction was the first reading. The bill has yet to reach a second reading.

For a period of more than 150 years, from the 1830s until 1997, First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were taken from their families and communities to residential schools, often far from their homes. Most were government-funded and run by Christian religious organizations.

The schools were designed to assimilate Indigenous children into Euro-Canadian culture. An estimated 150,000 children across Canada attended the schools and the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation has documented more than 4,000 who died while attending them.

On Sept. 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Kinew announced the province partnered with the City of Brandon to buy a popular campground property that was once part of the Brandon Residential School, which ran from 1895 until 1972 .

The site that became the campground included a former school cemetery, used from 1895 to 1912, the province said in a news release on the day the purchase was announced.

The property still contains the remains of children, the province said.

Kinew, who dedicated a memorial at the site on Sept. 30, said on Friday that such events help educate the public on residential schools.

"It's very well-documented. It's very historic. So let's make sure that we keep that history alive in our living memory as a province," he said.

Sioux Valley Dakota Nation, which owns the land where the school once stood, will guide decisions around the former cemetery and is working with university researchers to identify the more than 50 children it believes are buried at the site.

Rev. Stan McKay, who said his maternal grandparents were forced to attend the Brandon Residential School for a good part of their life and never talked about it, called the purchase of the cemetery land a “very important piece” of reconciliation.

"It was not a good place," McKay said the day of the province's announcement.

His eldest sisters also attended the Brandon school for two years, while he is a survivor of the Fisher River and Birtle residential schools.

The United Church of Canada was one of three church organizations that operated the Brandon school during its long history. Later, McKay later made history as the first Indigenous person to lead that church.

He said he nearly left the church after an "awakening" that he had been colonized by it. Elders, who also "had some difficulties with the church," encouraged him to stay and work within the system and be a part of helping it change, McKay said.

McKay would like to see more education in Manitoba schools around the residential school experience and have it localized to stories about the 18 schools that operated in the province.

Kinew, on Friday, agreed that would be a good idea and said much more is being done in schools now than in previous decades.

"How much did we learn about residential school in K-12 versus what a kid today learns? It's night and day in terms of being so much more," he said.

There is a need for those no longer in school to be educated as well, Kinew said.

"As we were preparing for Brandon … I was talking to some of my staff that I work with very closely — very smart people — and I pulled out the volume of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission that documents the child deaths. People were shocked. They didn't know [the number of deaths]," he said.

"So for sure there's more needs to be done in the K-12 system, but I think there's also a lot in the workplace, in churches, in sports, all the venues where we gather as Manitobans, where we need to keep this thing alive.

"The thing that we don't want to happen is for this to fade from our living memory, and then we forget, and then maybe some of the the negative lessons we should have learned start to re-emerge."

title: Anthropic bans 'cruel' behaviour against its Claude AI
summary: Anthropic has moved to bar users from treating its Claude AI system with needless cruelty, amid a growing philosophical debate over whether artificial intelligence can be conscious.
full_text:
Anthropic has moved to bar users from treating its Claude AI system with needless cruelty, amid a growing philosophical debate over whether artificial intelligence can be conscious.

The San Francisco-based AI lab updated its usage policy to include "a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behaviour toward our models."

"Claude's ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism," the policy states.

The updated policy does not explicitly cite so-called "model welfare," the idea that AI systems might deserve types of protection usually reserved for living things, but Anthropic and its executives have openly entertained the concept.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Already last year, the company said it was giving Claude the ability to end conversations in rare, extreme cases of "persistently harmful or abusive user interactions."

Then in February, CEO Dario Amodei told The New York Times he was unsure whether AI models could be conscious.

"We don't know if the models are conscious. But we're open to the idea that it could be," Mr Amodei said.

Science fiction and popular culture have been fascinated for decades by the boundary between technology and human intelligence, but asking whether AI is conscious may be the wrong question, according to Jackson Stakeman, a general manager at Sparq, an Atlanta-based AI services provider.

"Consciousness is a trap. We can't prove it in each other. Debate it for AI and you go in circles," Mr Stakeman told AFP.

"The mirror is a better metaphor. These systems reflect what we put in, at scale. That's reason enough for the policy change" at Anthropic, he added.

Read more:

OpenAI sacks three safety researchers for 'breach of trust'

Some have rejected the idea of machine consciousness outright, including Pope Leo XIV and Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman.

"AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer," Mr Suleyman wrote in an essay last month.

"Granting rights and moral protections to a technological entity, one that looks to be on a path to be seismically more capable and intelligent than us, is a recipe for disaster," he wrote.

In a sermon delivered in Italian yesterday at St Peter's Basilica in Vatican City, the pope suggested machines lack a soul, saying they merely "compile data" quickly.

"The mind must not simply compile data - as an algorithm now does more quickly than we can," the pontiff said.

It must "recall lived experiences, which contain depths of meaning that only the human soul can recognise, and connect more deeply with the goodness of these experiences," the pope said.

title: Students are keeping their options open. Is the sector keeping up?
summary:
International students are weighing more options than ever, making flexibility, clarity and outcomes increasingly important to their decision-making, writes Simon Emmett.

The post Students are keeping their options open. Is the sector keeping up? appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
International student decision-making is becoming less linear. Faced with changing visa policies, rising costs and emerging study destinations, students are comparing more countries, institutions and pathways before deciding where to go.

The inaugural IELTS Voices research offers a window into how 8,395 recent and prospective IELTS test takers are navigating these choices. Each year, millions of test takers prepare seriously and invest significant effort in achieving their goals. The IELTS partners wanted to understand what drives that commitment, what test takers value and how we can better support their journeys.

One of the clearest findings from the research is the importance test takers place on flexibility. Two in five study-focused respondents are considering multiple destinations and building a portfolio of options.

This matters for universities because in a world of increasing choice and risk, students are looking for confidence. Confidence that their true English language ability will be recognised, that they are prepared for life abroad and that their hard work will translate into education and career opportunities.

Recognition is central to this confidence, with 82% of respondents saying they would prioritise an English test accepted by the widest range of institutions and authorities.

In a world of increasing choice and risk, students are looking for confidence

Outcomes are also a priority. Almost nine in 10 respondents said outcomes were as important, if not more important than cost. While this does not tell us how price influences the wider English language testing market, it shows that the IELTS test takers surveyed see value in a test result that opens more doors.

So how do universities make sure that the door to their institution is open for talented international students? As a starting point, universities can reduce unnecessary friction in the application process by making accepted tests, score thresholds and entry requirements clearly signposted on their websites, consistent and easy to understand.

While more than half of respondents felt the requirements were communicated clearly, among those who experienced challenges, the minimum score requirement was the most difficult to understand (28%). Around one in four respondents also reported difficulties understanding application pathways (25%), test validity periods (24%) and visa-related testing requirements (24%).

Universities must then consider that the value of English language testing extends far beyond results and recognition. The research revealed that 67% of IELTS test takers reported improved confidence in speaking, writing or both following test preparation. Many also felt more confident using English in daily life and international settings.

IELTS is therefore more than a hurdle to entry. For the test takers surveyed, it is an investment in skills they will continue to draw on throughout their lives. However, even students who prepare well for their test may not succeed without continued English language support. Universities that invest in language development as an ongoing part of the student experience will see better outcomes, compared to those that view proficiency as an admission requirement alone.

Understanding how factors such as ongoing language support and accepted English language tests relate to outcomes including retention, progression, academic performance and graduate pathways is critical in a globally competitive environment. By tracking these connections over time, universities can build a clear picture of what drives student success and make more informed decisions about where to focus their resources and support.

Universities that treat testing simply as a gatekeeping requirement risk attracting students without the preparation they need, while letting down those students who have worked hard to earn their place and have so much to offer.

About the author: Simon Emmett is chief partner officer for IDP Education, CEO of IDP UK and member of the IELTS Board. A highly experienced international education and technology leader, Simon has spent more than 25 years working with students, institutions, governments and sector partners to navigate an increasingly complex global education landscape.

In his leadership role for IELTS, the world’s leading high-stakes English language proficiency test, Simon works closely with IELTS partners – British Council and Cambridge University Press and Assessment – to support the ongoing development, integrity and global reach of one of the most trusted assessments in international education.

title: How Leaders Overcome IT Staffing Shortages Through Retention and Upskilling
summary:
The talent tension in higher ed has many dimensions. Attracting IT talent has been a long-standing challenge for a variety of reasons, including compensation, burnout due to workload demand and limited or unclear advancement pathways. 
As if those challenges weren’t enough, policy changes and enrollment trends have created a cascading effect. Research funding, declining international student enrollment and overall uncertainty are piled on to the difficulty IT leaders are already grappling with in hiring and keeping an adequate number of staff to meet the needs of their campus. Layoffs…
full_text:
Build New Technological Capabilities Within Your Current Team

Waving the “do more with less” banner is a reality for many IT leaders. An important exercise, therefore, is to audit the existing skills of your team. Accurately identifying your team's collective skills is the starting point for mapping emerging skills to the team you already have in place. With funding scarcities, IT leaders have an advantage when making a case for specific professional development that advances the entire unit.

READ MORE: A better-trained staff leads to stronger security in higher education.

This is also a lens through which new roles can be identified. Predicting job titles that may disappear or emerge is less important than identifying the capabilities the institution will require.

Consider how many roles are already folding in data literacy as an essential component of the job. A systems administrator, for example, may increasingly be expected to evaluate utilization, communicate costs, manage vendor performance or advise leaders on the value of cloud investments. The important point is not that every systems administrator must become a cloud ROI analyst, but that institutions should regularly update job descriptions to reflect the work employees are already being asked to do and provide the preparation needed to do that work well.

Turn the Org Chart Into a Professional Development Map for IT Leaders

Higher education IT leaders facing restructuring have an unexpected advantage: the chance to intentionally redesign job roles and responsibilities. Acknowledge and prioritize the evolving competencies your unit needs into an existing role rather than removing a role entirely. A redesigned organizational chart should reflect these new skill requirements explicitly.

Budget constraints are real, and relief isn't on the horizon. But that doesn't mean accepting stagnation. Instead, it creates the window to make strategic choices about where limited resources go. Prioritize training and development for the competencies most critical to your redesigned structure and make that training nonnegotiable in your budget allocation.

Three practical approaches can upskill and reskill your existing tech team without breaking an already-strained budget.

First, tie training and certifications directly to implementation projects. Rather than generic professional development, negotiate learning into the rollout of new systems. This way the training becomes immediately relevant and embedded in the implementation timeline.

Second, when you contract for platform or system implementations, build job shadowing into the vendor agreement. Pair your existing IT staff with the implementation expert; that continuity transfer is far more valuable than the contracted system expert handing off documentation after launch.

Finally, staff augmentation through contracting can itself be a development strategy when structured intentionally. Your people learn alongside the external expert sourced as part of the contract agreement rather than being sidelined during the transition.

UP NEXT: The 2027 EDUCAUSE Top 10 highlights an era of change.

What separates institutions that stagnate from those that adapt won't be the size of their IT budget, instead it will be whether leaders chose to invest in the people already on their team. That investment doesn't have to wait for a strategic planning cycle or a line-item approval. It can start this week, with a conversation about which systems administrator wants to learn cloud cost analysis, or which vendor contract could include a shadowing clause instead of a handoff document.

Institutions that come out ahead over the next five years probably won't have solved the hiring shortage; most won't, budgets being what they are. They'll simply have gotten better at recognizing the capacity within the teams they already have and building toward it intentionally instead of waiting for headcount that is unlikely to happen any time soon.

title: Beyond net zero: a journey towards ‘regenerative sustainability’
summary: The post Beyond net zero: a journey towards ‘regenerative sustainability’ appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Scott Davidson, Head of Sustainability at the University of Edinburgh, shares how the institution is moving from damage limitation to active restoration.

For decades, the global sustainability narrative has been dominated by reducing the harm we do. Whether that’s reducing (not reversing) deforestation, lessening climate change, or slowing ecological damage. The traditional narrative of “do less harm…” has often missed “…and repair harm done”. Net Zero is the prime example of do less harm without repairing harm done, acknowledging that huge harm has already happened with worrying amounts still to come. As we face an intensifying environmental polycrisis, where climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution and water issues reinforce one another, focusing only on doing less harm via net zero is no longer enough – we’ve gone too far for that.

Over the last few years at the University of Edinburgh, we’ve been asking ourselves a difficult question: if every organisation acted as we plan to, would it be sufficient to achieve the future we seek for all? Where the answer was no, we’ve challenged ourselves to think harder about action that is sufficient.

This reflection led to the launch of our new Regenerative sustainability strategy 2025-40. This isn’t just an update to how we do sustainability and net zero; it is a fundamental shift from sustainability as “do less harm” focused on Estate Net Zero, to sustainability that actually tackles the challenges we face. We view this through a lens of materiality, prioritising those areas where we can have our largest impact, ie through our teaching and learning and our research and innovation, underpinned by our people and culture. When we do consider operations, we target Net Negative Carbon, ecological regeneration of an area of land five times the size of our campus, and a step change on our impacts on chemical pollution and water.

Our ambition is to become a truly regenerative university: one that actively repairs natural systems to ensure a net positive environmental and social impact.

What does regenerative look like in practice?

Our strategy, spanning 2025 to 2040, moves beyond a largely estate-based focus to leverage our greatest assets: our people, our research and our teaching. We are committing to all students, regardless of degree studied, having access to meaningful study of climate and nature; to more than trebling the amount of climate and nature research we undertake. Our Net Negative Carbon commitment follows science aligned pathways beyond estates to include everything we buy and all of our travel, and our ecological regeneration targets apply both to our campus and to land across Scotland.

One part of this ambition includes our Forest and Peatland Programme: a £50 million initiative that is sequestering 1 million tonnes of our unavoidable scope 3 CO2e emissions by actively regenerating 5,600 hectares of land across Scotland. This is an area more than 240 times the size of Edinburgh’s Meadows, for those of you who have strolled down its cherry-blossom avenues.

Crucially, this isn’t just about offsetting carbon; it’s about nature, local communities, and the creation of living labs where students and researchers can engage directly with nature restoration, bridging the gap between academic theory and tangible impact.

Year 1: Early impacts and lessons learnt

While the strategy is long-term, our first year of implementation has already yielded valuable insights and early wins that other institutions might find useful.

Culture is the engine: Strategy without a sufficient number of people bought in enough to prioritise it will not succeed. Achieving that buy in requires an intentional and pro-active approach to the culture that supports those people, and it can’t be achieved just through communications. For example, we are changing our physical campus to better reflect our regenerative ambitions through “Wild Campus”, and on campus and in-school signage. We launched a behaviour change platform and expanded our training ambitions significantly. We have moved from training 500 staff and students annually to 5,000 every year in Carbon Literacy, Biodiversity Literacy, and the Circular Economy, and from engaging in the hundreds to engaging over 10,000 last year. The uptake has been enthusiastic, proving that when you empower your community with knowledge, they lead the charge.

Embedding across the curriculum: We are making rapid progress on our goal to ensure every student, regardless of their degree, accesses meaningful climate and nature learning. By integrating these themes into learning outcomes rather than treating them as add-ons, we are graduating changemakers equipped to tackle the polycrisis in any sector they enter.

Research into action: Our Edinburgh Earth Initiative is catalysing transdisciplinary work that turns research into real-world solutions. We’ve more than doubled our volume of research in climate and nature already, with plenty more to come. From spin-outs like SeaWarm, which provides renewable heating from water sources, to projects tackling greenwashing in global accounting standards, and Mi-Algae which is reducing wild fish consumption, carbon and other impacts using whisky bi-products to create marine Omega 3-rich algae, our research is directly informing policy and industry practice.

The challenge of the polycrisis

It is not possible to solve climate change without resilient ecological systems including healthy oceans which in turn are impacted by climate change, chemical pollution and water scarcity and quality. Our approach, informed by the Planetary Boundaries Framework, ensures we don’t silo our efforts.

Furthermore, we recognise that this is a global justice issue. The communities least responsible for emissions often bear the brunt of climate impacts, the tragic flash flood in Nepal being the latest example of many. Our strategy is rooted in climate justice, ensuring our transition is equitable and that our research and partnerships support vulnerable communities globally.

Join the conversation

The journey to regeneration is complex, and no single university has all the answers, but at a time when a university’s social license to operate is being questioned, demonstrating the critical role we play in tackling these crises is important. We hope that sharing our challenges, our failures and our successes is helpful to our colleagues across the higher education sector.

To dive deeper into our approach, discuss the practicalities of embedding regenerative principles in your own institution, and explore how we are measuring our progress, I invite you to join our upcoming webinar series in collaboration with the International Sustainable Campus Network, beginning on Wednesday 21 October 2026. We will be unpacking the strategy, sharing case studies from our research, teaching, operations and governance, and discussing how to foster a culture of regenerative sustainability on campus.

Register here for the Regenerative Sustainability Webinar Series

We hope this series sparks new ideas and collaborations across the sector. After all, if we are to secure a thriving future, we must learn from each other and work together.

Scott Davidson is the Head of Sustainability and Deputy Director of Social Responsibility and Sustainability at the University of Edinburgh. He leads the development and delivery of the University’s Regenerative Sustainability Strategy, focusing embedding sustainability across teaching, research, operations, governance and the University’s culture.

title: Schools crisis in France: Investment fails to inspire confidence
summary: For weeks, schoolchildren in France have been protesting the failing education system. Compared to many other countries, France invests heavily in education but critics say that the funds are not distributed fairly.
full_text:
Rats in the toilets, leaking roofs, broken heating systems: Cellphone videos filmed by French schoolchildren and circulating on social media bear witness to the dilapidated infrastructure in many educational institutions across France.

At the Lycee Paul Eluard in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, a center of the current protests, young people have reported that there are vermin in the building, and say burst pipes are a regular occurrence. In nearby Pantin, pupils complained that windows couldn't be opened, even when temperatures soared to 40 degrees Celsius (over 104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer.

Pupils also complain of overcrowded classrooms and frequently cancelled lessons.

The protests, which have erupted all over the country, show no sign of coming to an end.

Problems of centralization

Yet, by EU standards, France invests a substantial amount in its education system — 6.7% of its GDP. The fact that this investment has not translated into a better learning environment may be partly attributable to the way responsibilities are divided.

The central government in Paris mainly deals with paying teachers, and setting national curricula. But the responsibility for maintaining school buildings lies with France's various levels of local government. For elementary schools, the administration responsible is the municipality; for "colleges" (lower secondary schools, ages 11–15) it is the wider department, and for lycees (upper secondary schools, ages 15–18) it is the region.

Depending on the region, the local authorities have different financial possibilities at their disposal, and must plan renovation projects themselves. Progress on making improvements is often very slow as a result. In addition, more than two-thirds of their budget is already allocated to staffing costs and pension payments, leaving relatively little room for investment.

Dilapidated infrastructure

Over 80% of elementary school buildings in France are more than 50 years old. An estimated 10 to 20% of all school buildings are considered to be in serious need of renovation. In many instances, politicians have been trying to address the problem. Ile-de-France, which covers Paris and the region surrounding it, approved a 10-year program of renovation and expansion for the period 2017 to 2027 at a cost of €6.6 billion ($7.4 billion).

According to the local authorities, two-thirds of upper secondary pupils now attend a new school, or one that has been renovated. But even after mold has been removed and roofs repaired, it is still rare for buildings to have effective protection against the summer heat. It is also a bitter irony that some buildings newly constructed at considerable expense, or renovated just a few years earlier, have been damaged in the recent protests.

Macron tried in vain to address problem

Imbalances are also evident in ongoing education expenditure. While France invests a comparatively large amount in upper secondary education, according to OECD calculations Paris spends less per primary school pupil than the average for industrialized countries. Education researchers emphasize that it is precisely these early years that lay the foundation for subsequent academic success.

The governments put in place by French President Emmanuel Macron have attempted to address this imbalance. Since 2017, class sizes in the first years of primary school have been halved in socially disadvantaged areas, and around 16,000 additional teaching posts created.

Amid the ongoing protests, the government has said it now intends to recruit more than 3,000 supply teachers at short notice. French Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced that software would be used to identify schools that are in a particularly difficult situation.

These announcements are the government's first concrete response to the demands of the students, who have been demonstrating for almost two weeks now, calling for better facilities in secondary schools, more supply teachers and greater investment in the education system generally.

Increasing deficiencies

The latest scores for the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) program for international student assessment (Pisa), which were published in September, illustrate the scale of the problems in the education system. According to the results, more than one in three 15-year-olds in France no longer achieve a basic level of competence in mathematics, for example.

Macron's reform of the upper secondary education system has also been criticized. The abolition of academic streaming in favor of specialist subjects selected by the individual was meant to give pupils greater freedom of choice. However, the large number of possible subject combinations make it difficult to timetable lessons. Students complain that they have too many free periods and longer school days.

The problems also extend to universities. A lecturer at a Paris university described a seminar attended by 50 students — so many that they have to fetch chairs from other rooms or sit on the floor. So far, she said, the university administration had done nothing about it.

Cancelled lessons

Compared with pupils in other EU countries, French schoolchildren have a high number of teaching hours per school year — on paper, at least. But the French Court of Accounts recorded that 9% of lessons at state colleges were cancelled in the 2023–24 school year. A study from the school year 2024–25 suggests that only around 12% of lessons cancelled at short notice are covered by other teachers.

The relatively low salaries of French teachers compared to those in neighboring countries are also a problem. OECD data shows that after 15 years in the profession teachers at lower secondary schools in France only earn about half as much as their German counterparts.

Broken promises of equality

France takes pride in its republican model of education, which is supposed to provide all children with equal opportunities, irrespective of their background. In reality, academic success in France is much more dependent on parents' socioeconomic circumstances than in many other countries. This is also apparent in that children from poorer families are far more likely to be affected by the cancellation of lessons.

The government's financial room for maneuver is currently restricted by the country's precarious budgetary situation. Although the draft budget for 2027 includes an additional €1.2 billion for the Ministry of Education, there are also plans to cut teaching posts, on the grounds that pupil numbers are falling.

Protests in the run-up to the presidential election

It's not just videos of dilapidated school buildings that are circulating on social media. As the discontent has spread, there is also footage of demonstrations where people carry placards with political slogans that have little to do with education policy. Some videos show burning barricades and clashes with the police, which faces accusations of usingdisproportionate force.

Some members of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party have associated themselves with the protesting students. Lawmakers have appeared at school blockades and shared related videos. The government has accused LFI of deliberately exploiting young people's anger for political purposes, an allegation that the party rejects.

With the French presidential election just six months away, the protests over the crisis in education are evolving into a power struggle.

This article was originally published in German.

title: Agil und strukturiert: eine Umgebung für KI-gestütztes Lernen
summary: KI hilft beim Einstieg in fremde Fachgebiete, irrt dabei aber unbemerkt. Wie sieht ein agiler Lernprozess aus, der davor schützt?
full_text:
Inhaltsverzeichnis

Entwicklerinnen und Entwickler, die Testfälle für Systeme schreiben, die sie nur oberflächlich verstehen, produzieren Testfälle, die nur die Oberfläche treffen. Sich in eine Fachdomäne einzuarbeiten ist daher ebenso erforderlich wie Kenntnisse von Äquivalenzklassen, Grenzwertanalyse und risikobasierter Priorisierung. Einarbeitung in neue Themen steht auch an, wenn etwa ein neues Testautomatisierungstool eingeführt wird, für das Bestehen einer Zertifikatsprüfung oder die Vorbereitung für eine neue Rolle, beispielsweise wenn eine Testerin Testmanagerin werden möchte.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Eine KI-gestützte Lernumgebung kann bei all diesen Themen helfen, aber nur mit dem richtigen Prozess und einem technischen Rahmen. Dieser Artikel zeigt den Lernprozess sowie den Aufbau der Lernumgebung mit Claude Code, Zettelkasten und Skills. Am Ende beschreibt er drei Lernprojekte aus der Praxis. Der gezeigte Aufbau ist eine Idee des Autors und wird in dessen Firma bereits von Kolleginnen und Kollegen genutzt. Die vorgestellte Umgebung kann in regulierten Umgebungen laufen, dient aber nicht dazu, Lernthemen zu bearbeiten, die interne Dokumente erfordern.

Der Prozess: agiles Lernen mit KI

Der klassische Lernweg ist, ein Buch von der ersten bis zur letzten Seite zu lesen oder einen Onlinekurs Lektion für Lektion durchzuarbeiten. Das kostet aber viel Zeit und liefert oft breites Wissen, von dem für das konkrete Projekt nur ein kleiner Teil benötigt wird. Entwicklerinnen und Entwickler, die ein 100-seitiges Anforderungsdokument in zwei Wochen so weit verstehen müssen, um sinnvolle Testfälle erstellen zu können, können sich diesen Weg nicht leisten.

Nils Röttger

Nils Röttger hat mehr als 15 Jahre Erfahrung im Bereich Ausbildung und Coaching. Seit 2008 arbeitet er bei der imbus AG in Möhrendorf, aktuell als Senior Consultant, Projektleiter und KI-Experte in Kundenprojekten. Er ist mitverantwortlich für den Bereich Künstliche Intelligenz. Außerdem ist er Lernarchitekt und Product Owner für das Agile Lernen. In seinen vielen Vorträgen auf Konferenzen und als Autor von Büchern oder Fachartikeln beschäftigt er sich immer wieder mit aktuellen Themen rund um KI, Lernen und Testen.

Agiles Lernen geht anders vor und stellt dazu sechs Fragen. Am Anfang steht folgende: Was muss der Testende am Ende können, und bis wann? Ein Ziel wie „Ich möchte die Domäne Wetter besser verstehen“ ist zu beliebig, um damit zu arbeiten. Ein Ziel wie „einzelne Wetter-Begriffe wie Hoch und Tief einordnen“ gibt dem Lernpfad eine Richtung. Daraus entsteht ein Lernpfad aus kurzen Sprints, kein fertiger Lernplan. Nach jedem Sprint folgt ein Review. Dort klären die Lernenden, ob das Gelernte schon für den nächsten Schritt reicht oder ob eine weitere Runde benötigt wird. Am Ende benutzt die Lernende das Wissen direkt in ihrer täglichen Arbeit.

Die zweite Frage ist die nach der Zeit. Ein Zeithorizont zwingt zur Priorität. Wer drei Wochen Zeit zum Lernen hat, lernt anders als der, dem dafür drei Monate zur Verfügung stehen.

Die dritte Frage betrifft die Länge eines Sprints. Eine Woche ist ein guter Standardwert. Zwei Wochen können sinnvoll sein, wenn sich der Stoff schwer portionieren lässt. Dazu kommt die Zeit, die pro Sprint wirklich zur Verfügung steht, in jedem Sprint zum Beispiel zwei Stunden. Diese Stunden addieren sich nicht wie auf einem Konto. Acht Wochen mit je einer Stunde ergeben eben keinen Achtstundentag, und das ist ein Vorteil. In den Pausen zwischen den Einheiten arbeitet der Kopf am Stoff weiter, ganz nebenbei, sodass er beim nächsten Sprint fester sitzt als nach einem einzigen langen Block.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Die vierte Frage ist die nach Ort und Zeitpunkt. Gelernt wird im Zug, am Schreibtisch, in Blöcken von einer Stunde oder in kurzen Einheiten am Morgen. Dazu gehört auch, ob es feste Termine gibt oder ob die Sprints nach Bedarf laufen.

Die fünfte Frage betrifft die Lernform. Manche Themen erschließen sich über eine angeleitete Schulung schneller. Andere erarbeitet der Lernende im Selbststudium, mithilfe der KI und den ausgewählten Quellen. Auch eine Mischform ist möglich. Der eigentliche Wert dieser Bauweise liegt in der Frage, die sie jedes Mal aufwirft. Container wie Podman im rootless-Modus sind schlanker und starten in Sekunden, teilen sich aber den Kernel mit dem Host. Bubblewrap packt einzelne Prozesse feingranular in eine Sandbox. Auch der Sandbox-Modus von Claude Code unter Linux arbeitet damit.

Welche Lösung am sichersten ist, hängt vom Blickwinkel ab. Ein Container spart Aufwand und Startzeit, teilt sich aber den Kernel mit dem Host. Eine VM zieht dagegen die härtere Grenze, mit eigenem Kernel. Sicherheit ist nicht das einzige Kriterium, Bedienbarkeit und Wartung zählen auch. Dieser Artikel zeigt die Lösung mit VirtualBox, weil ein eigener Kernel die härteste der klassischen Grenzen zieht und ein Snapshot die ganze VM nach einem Experiment auf Knopfdruck zurücksetzt. Aufsetzen und Konfiguration kosten allerdings Zeit.

Die erste Ebene ist die Wissensbasis, nach Themen sortiert. Ein Ordner beispielsweise für die Wetter-App, einer für Python, einer für die ISTQB-Vorbereitung. Ein Thema überlebt viele Projekte, deshalb entscheidet das Thema über die Ablage. Eine Notiz zur Wetter-App taugt in zwei Jahren für einen ganz anderen Zweck. Die zweite Ebene sind die Projekte, die aus dieser Basis schöpfen, zum Beispiel das Lernen für ein Zertifikat. Das trennt das Material von den Werkstücken. Für ein neues Lernthema entsteht einfach ein neuer Ordner, ohne dass die Struktur umgebaut werden muss.

Welche zwei Notizen zueinander gehören, entscheidet die Testerin, das Skript stellt nur die technische Verknüpfung her. Wer diese drei durcheinander wirft, schreibt entweder ständig dasselbe in jeden Prompt oder überlädt die Projektanweisung mit Dingen, die dort nicht hingehören.

Eine liegt auf Höhe des geteilten Ordners und gilt für alles darunter. Eine zweite kommt im Wetter-App-Ordner hinzu, sobald Claude Code dort arbeitet, und trägt das bei, was nur dieses Thema angeht. Beide gelten dann gemeinsam. Über den Projektbaum hinaus gibt es weitere Ablageorte, eine persönliche Datei im Heimatverzeichnis für alle Projekte und eine von der IT verwaltete für unternehmensweite Vorgaben.

Ein Skill ist ein Ordner mit einer SKILL.md-Datei, dazu bei Bedarf Skripte oder weitere Ressourcen. Die Projektanweisung liest Claude Code immer. So lässt sich für ein einzelnes Projekt eine abweichende Fassung hinterlegen, während die persönliche in allen anderen Projekten unangetastet bleibt.

Skills über die Themenordner zu verteilen, ergibt dagegen keinen Sinn. Claude Code findet einen Skill über seine Beschreibung, egal wo er im Baum liegt. Faustregel: Was über mehrere Projekte hinweg wiederkehrt, gehört in einen Skill; was nur ein einzelnes Thema betrifft, gehört in die Projektanweisung. Ein Skill für ein wiederkehrendes Rollenspiel wandert an den zentralen Ort. Das Fachwissen über die Wetter-App steht in der CLAUDE.md des Themenordners.

Ein Ordner, zwei Architekturen: Der geteilte Ordner verklammert die beiden Architekturen dieses Artikels. Die Sicherheitsarchitektur aus dem vorangegangenen Abschnitt sagt, was überhaupt auf den Share darf. Die Wissensarchitektur beschreibt, wie das Erlaubte dort geordnet ist. Es ist derselbe Ordner, aus zwei Blickwinkeln betrachtet.

Wer seine Skills und Anweisungen zusammen mit dem Wissen auf dem Share halten will, damit sie vom Host aus bearbeitbar bleiben und mit der VM wandern, legt sie projektgebunden an. Wer sie über alle Umgebungen hinweg teilen will, nimmt die persönliche Variante im Home in Kauf.
